newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council close to authorizing force for Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council close to authorizing force for Zaire.

text.p: The Security Council was expected to adopt a resolution late on Friday or Saturday authorising a multinational force, not under U.N. command, to halt what Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali called "genocide by starvation" in Eastern Zaire.

After consultations on a draft aimed at establishing conditions for food and other aid to reach more than a million refugees from ethnic conflicts, council members scheduled another closed-door session later to complete the text.
The resolution, drafted mainly by France, could be adopted on)Friday night or Saturday, council members said.

Boutros-Ghali, who attended the consulations to press for speedy council action, said members' reactions "proved that they want to act. And I hope that in the next 24 hours they will act and that they will adopt a resolution in favour of a rapid action in eastern Zaire."

Referring to mass killings in Rwanda in 1994, when up to a million people were butchered in ethnic slaughter, the secretary-general said: "Two years ago we have been confronted by a genocide by the Hutus against the Tutsis.

"Now we are confronted by a new genocide -- I will call it a genocide by starvation. Because they are dying, because they are not able to receive food, nor medicaments nor clean water. So we must act, and we must act immediately," he said.
Council members gave no indication of their countries' possible contributions to the proposed force, whose size has not yet been determined.
France and Spain have already said they could send 1,000 men each as part of a 5,000-strong force, though Rwanda's Tutsi government is mistrustful of France as an ally of the ousted Hutu government.
Boutros-Ghali said the proposed multinational contingent would have to use force to protect humanitarian supplies against looting and attack, and to protect the refugees.
Hundreds of thousands of people fled to Eastern Zaire after the mass killings in Rwanda and to escape a continuing conflict between Hutus and Tutsis in neighbouring Burundi.

The Rwandan refugees include still-armed members of the former Hutu-led army and militia responsible for the 1994 genocide who fear retribution if they return home and have used force to prevent other Hutus from being repatriated.
The situation is further complicated by fighting between the Zairean army and Zairean ethnic Tutsis, who are backed by the Rwandan army.

In a letter to the Security Council on Thursday Boutros-Ghali said a multinational force, authorised by the council but not under U.N. command, was the best option because it would take too long to deploy a U.N. peacekeeping force or a force fielded by countries of the region, which in any case would need financial and logistical support.

But he said the crisis was not only a humanitarian one since recent events proved peace and security in the region would not be restored unless the refugee crisis caused by the internal conflicts in Rwanda and Burundi were resolved.

"It will therefore be necessary to ensure that the short-term response does not re-create conditions in which refugees can again be intimidated by those who, for political reasons, do not want them to return to their home countries," Boutros-Ghali said.
"On the contrary, the international community's response to this humanitarian crisis must mark the beginning of a new programme of repatriation."
